content_voiceover: This flowchart gives you a practical approach when you suspect an inherited platelet disorder. You always start with a CBC and peripheral blood smear. If the platelet count is normal, you check von Willebrand studies first, and if those are normal too, you move on to platelet aggregation testing, which can show a nonspecific pattern pointing toward acquired or mild disorders, or a significant abnormal pattern that splits into granule release defects like storage pool disease, or surface protein defects like Glanzmann thrombasthenia or Bernard Soulier syndrome. If instead the patient has thrombocytopenia, the mean platelet volume becomes your key branch point. Large platelets with an M P V under twelve suggest MYH9 related disorder, Paris Trousseau Jacobsen syndrome, or twenty two q deletion syndrome, and these go straight to genetic analysis. Normal sized platelets point toward bone marrow failure syndromes such as congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenia absent radius, or familial platelet disorder with AML predisposition, which need a bone marrow study before genetics. Small platelets under six femtoliters should make you think of Wiskott Aldrich syndrome or X linked thrombocytopenia, worked up with immune function studies.
keypoints: Start every workup with CBC and peripheral smear
Normal platelet count pathway checks von Willebrand studies then aggregation
Thrombocytopenia pathway branches by mean platelet volume
Large platelets suggest MYH9 related disorder or Paris Trousseau syndrome
Small platelets suggest Wiskott Aldrich syndrome or X linked thrombocytopenia
keypoint_voiceover: Remember this algorithm by starting with CBC and smear, then splitting into normal platelet count versus thrombocytopenia. For thrombocytopenia, mean platelet volume is the key branch point, large platelets suggest MYH9 related disease, normal size suggests marrow failure syndromes, and small platelets point toward Wiskott Aldrich or X linked thrombocytopenia.
